subtopics.title: What Development Means — and What It Does Not

questions.question: Development is best defined as:
options: The process by which people's quality of life improves — income together with health, schooling, safety, freedom and dignity
An increase in a country's total output of goods and services
The construction of new factories and highways
A rise in the value of a country's exports

questions.question: Why can an economy grow while its people do not develop?
options: Growth always causes prices to rise faster than wages
Growth measures a larger total of goods and services, and that new wealth can gather in a handful of accounts instead of improving lives
Growth only counts agricultural production
Growth and development are opposites by definition

questions.question: A smelter shift-worker earns a solid wage while the plant's fumes settle over his street. He has:
options: A poor standard of living and a high quality of life
Both a high standard of living and a high quality of life
A decent standard of living but a compromised quality of life, because quality of life includes health and environment beyond income
Neither, because the terms only apply to countries

questions.question: India, Malaysia, Turkey and South Africa — countries whose factories rose within a generation — are classified as:
options: MEDCs
LEDCs
First World countries
NICs — newly industrialised countries

subtopics.title: Measuring Development in Money: GDP, GNP and the Gini Coefficient

questions.question: The BMW plant at Rosslyn outside Pretoria counts inside:
options: South Africa's GDP but Germany's GNP, because GDP follows where production happens while GNP follows the nationality of the owner
Germany's GDP but South Africa's GNP
Both countries' GDP at the same time
Neither country's national accounts

questions.question: When MTN earns revenue from its networks in Nigeria, that activity belongs to:
options: South Africa's GDP and Nigeria's GNP
Nigeria's GDP and South Africa's GNP, because the production happens on Nigerian soil but the company is South African
South Africa's GDP only
Nigeria's GDP and Nigeria's GNP

questions.question: Why do geographers prefer GDP per capita to total GDP for comparing countries?
options: Per capita figures remove the effect of inflation
Per capita figures include social indicators automatically
Dividing by population gives output per person, so a populous country no longer looks rich merely because it is big
Total GDP cannot be measured accurately

questions.question: South Africa's Gini coefficient of about 0,63 shows that:
options: The country's total output is shrinking
The average income is lower than Mozambique's
Prices are rising faster than in the Nordic countries
Income is shared extremely unequally, so a middle-income average coexists with mass poverty that per capita figures conceal

subtopics.title: Beyond Money: HDI and the Social Indicators

questions.question: Why is the infant mortality rate the most sensitive development indicator?
options: A baby survives only when everything works simultaneously — antenatal care, vaccines, sanitation and household income — so the figure reflects the whole system
Births are the only events every country records
It changes faster than any other statistic
It is determined entirely by hospital spending

questions.question: The three dimensions averaged into the Human Development Index are:
options: GDP, GNP and the Gini coefficient
Health via life expectancy, education via years of schooling, and income via GNI per capita
Employment, exports and electrification
Population growth, urbanisation and literacy

questions.question: South Africa's HDI of about 0,71 sits below its income ranking chiefly because:
options: Years of schooling are the lowest in the region
The index excludes mining income
The health dimension — life expectancy in the mid-sixties — pulls the combined score down despite relatively strong income and schooling
The rand's exchange rate distorts the calculation

questions.question: The HDI's designed advantage over GDP-based measures is that:
options: It is updated more frequently
It uses a wider numerical scale
It only measures the richest countries
No country can purchase a top score while its people die young, so it exposes the gap between wealth and wellbeing that GDP cannot see

questions.question: The Brandt line of 1980:
options: Separated a wealthy global North from a poorer global South, dipping to include Australia and New Zealand — a first sketch that has blurred as countries like Singapore rose
Divided the world along the equator
Marked the boundary between capitalist and communist states
Remains a perfectly accurate map of world development

questions.question: Calling development a continuum means:
options: Development happens continuously without interruption
Every country occupies its own position on an unbroken line from least to most developed, with no clean break where a boundary could honestly be drawn
All countries develop at the same speed
Only two categories of country exist

questions.question: Umhlanga's glass offices and Inanda's informal settlements belonging to one eThekwini metro demonstrate that:
options: The Brandt line passes through Durban
Coastal cities are always wealthy
Development differences run within a country as steeply as between countries, which is why the Gini coefficient matters
Municipal boundaries determine development

questions.question: The balanced, evidence-led classification of South Africa is:
options: A fully developed MEDC because of its financial markets
An LEDC because of its unemployment rate
A country that cannot be classified at all
A developing, newly industrialised country holding pockets of MEDC prosperity and pockets of LEDC deprivation, argued from income, HDI, unemployment and inequality

questions.question: In the two-streets picture of the Karoo town, development is:
options: The long work of bringing the second street up to the first — tar, taps, vaccines and teachers, not simply money
Relocating everyone from the second street to the first
Raising incomes on the first street even further
Building a bypass around the town

questions.question: The farm foreman who earns well but drinks from a contaminated borehole shows:
options: That rural wages are always too low
A standard of living without the matching quality of life, because quality of life adds health, safety and clean water to what income buys
That boreholes raise quality of life
That the two terms mean the same thing

questions.question: The solar farm that lifts the district's output while its dividends flow overseas and the town gains three jobs illustrates:
options: Development without growth
Sustainable development
Growth without development — rain on the catchment that never reaches the taps
Both growth and development at once

questions.question: In the cricket picture, dividing a club's total runs by its number of players stands for:
options: Calculating GDP per capita — output per person — so club size stops distorting the comparison
Calculating the Gini coefficient
Converting GDP into GNP
Adjusting the total for inflation

questions.question: Runs scored at your home ground by anyone, versus runs scored by your contracted players at any ground, stands for:
options: Exports versus imports
GDP — production inside the borders — versus GNP, production by a country's own citizens and companies wherever they operate
Standard of living versus quality of life
Total GDP versus GDP per capita

questions.question: The team that totals one hundred and ten runs, with one batter on ninety-one and ten others sharing nineteen, is the analogy for:
options: A rapidly growing economy
A country with a trade surplus
South Africa's inequality — a respectable average income beside a Gini coefficient of about 0,63
A country with a strong currency

questions.question: The paired sentence worth memorising is:
options: The Gini sizes the cake; the average cuts it
Both numbers measure the same thing twice
Neither number says anything about distribution
The average sizes each person's slice of the cake; the Gini tells you how the knife actually cut

subtopics.title: The Report Card With Three Subjects

questions.question: The three subjects on the HDI report card are:
options: Health graded by life expectancy, education graded by years of schooling, and income per person
Exports, savings and currency strength
Agriculture, mining and manufacturing
GDP, GNP and the Gini coefficient

questions.question: Why can no country 'cram the money subject' to top the HDI class?
options: Income is excluded for wealthy countries
The index deliberately averages three dimensions, so a high income cannot buy a top score while health or schooling lag behind
The health mark counts double
The index is capped for oil exporters

questions.question: A steadily falling infant mortality rate is development you can trust because:
options: It directly increases GDP per capita
It proves hospitals are being privatised
Keeping an infant alive needs clinics, vaccines, clean water and food all working at once, so a falling line means the whole system is improving
It only reflects the number of doctors

questions.question: On the staircase picture of world development, South Africa stands:
options: On the top step beside Switzerland
On the bottom step beside Niger
Off the staircase entirely
Mid-staircase — a developing country with one foot on a high step and one on a low one, defended with the indicators
